newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-S.African sells ultimate adrenaline high, very high.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-S.African sells ultimate adrenaline high, very high.

text.p: The glossy black British Aerospace Buccaneer S2BF bomber takes its place in a line-up of jumbo jets full of tourists waiting to take off from Cape Town's international airport.

Menacing-looking even without the wingload of weapons carried while in military service, the twin-engined jet screams down the runway and streaks off towards South Africa's coast for a fast sea-level flight to the coastal town of George.

"There is nothing, nothing at all quite like the thrill of flying this sort of heavy metal," said Mike Beachy Head, not yet 40 and retired from serious business to create and run Classic Jets South Africa.
Beachy Head insists that Classic Jets is as much a business as the courier airline company he sold last May to finance the venture, but the atmosphere around the hangar belies his claim.
No one should have this much fun at work.
"It started off as fun and it still is fun, but I have been quite amazed at the fascination of the general public for this thing...and when people are this interested there's obviously a business.
"This is the ultimate high for those people who have done everything else," Beachy Head said.
BORED ENTREPRENEUR BUYS THREE JETS BY PHONE
A friend who recognised that the entrepreneur was bored with the usual collection of big boy's toys, sent him a Sotheby's auction catalogue listing Royal Air Force jets coming up for sale.
Beachy Head joined the auction by telephone from his home in Cape Town's exclusive old-money suburb of Kirstenbosch, planning to buy a Hawker Hunter.
"While I was talking to the guy at Sotheby's he sort of talked me into the bidding for a couple of others and I did. And I got them. I got three," he recalled.
Now there was going to be serious competition for his speedboat, Italian motorcycle, off-road truck and German sports car scattered about the garden.
"I like going fast and I'm not much of a person for the straight and level stuff," he said.
Beachy Head was an experienced aerobatic pilot but had never flown a jet. And it was far from clear whether any of the planes he had bought could be made to fly again.
He qualified in England while British classic jet enthusiast Barry Pover, an experienced jet engineer, began work on his planes.
With Pover's encouragement, Beachy Head has expanded his collection to 10 planes and his company has a book value of 14 million pounds ($24 million).

"The operational cost of these aircraft is such that if you don't make money out of it, it's impossible. The movement will die. We cannot keep these aircraft flying unless we have some way of covering the expenses and building the fleet," he said.
COMPANY CAN TAKE OFF ONLY IN SOUTH AFRICA

The opportunity to make a business of his new enthusiasm arose when he and Pover were able to persuade South African aviation authorities to license a civilian company flying privately owned military jets.
"Our authorities in South Africa...are a very strict, very professional, very august body of people, but they do have an open mind in regard to what we can fly and can't fly.
"South Africa is the only country in the world where we can fly these aircraft on a civilian register as a civilian outfit," he said.
At the start of 1997, Beachy Head had the world's only flying Buccaneer, a two-seater Hawker Hunter T8 advanced jet trainer and a single-seater Hunter operational in Cape Town.
A twin-engined Lightning T5 was being reassembled in Britain after final certification, three others were being prepared for inspection and another Buccaneer was about to return to South Africa.
For a roundtrip price of $35,000 per person, Classic Jets will fly clients first class from anywhere in the world, put them up in five star hotels and give them five unforgettable flights.
Among the thrills are an aerobatic routine in a Hunter to a vertical afterburner lob to 60,000 feet (18,300 metres) in a Lightning with a descent at twice the speed of sound.
"We target a very, very general market and what we offer is the thrill of a lifetime. There is nothing really to top it," Beachy Head said.
